title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.

report.summary: A new benchmark, MedConstBench, shows that the ethical "constitution" written into a medical LLM changes its moral trade-offs in ways that vary by model and by ethical dimension.
report.background: Open-weight LLMs are increasingly run locally by clinics, insurers and individual clinicians, where the vendor can no longer tune behaviour after release. In that setting, the main lever over how a model answers an ethical dilemma is the constitution: the written policy, system prompt or alignment document that defines its values and priorities. Constitutional AI and similar 'deliberative alignment' methods made this a mainstream technique, and model providers now publish documents like Anthropic's constitution or OpenAI's Model Spec. Yet medical evaluation has concentrated on factual accuracy: exam-style question sets, hallucination rates, diagnostic recall. Ethics, when measured at all, is treated as a fixed property of a model rather than a variable you can change. That leaves a practical gap, since real clinical dilemmas rarely have a single correct answer; they require balancing autonomy against beneficence, or privacy against harm prevention. MedConstBench addresses that gap by making the constitution an experimental variable rather than a constant.
key_points: The core move is methodological: MedConstBench treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable rather than a fixed feature of a model. The authors evaluate ten open-source LLMs under four different constitutions, so differences in ethical behaviour can be attributed to the policy text itself instead of to model size, training data or vendor defaults.

Scoring is organised around Beauchamp's four principles of biomedical ethics: respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. Judgements come from a human-calibrated multi-model peer review process, an attempt to scale nuanced ethical grading without pretending that a single automated metric can capture moral trade-offs.

The benchmark ships its own dataset, MedDilemma, a collection of clinical dilemmas written for this purpose. Together with the constitution-swapping design, it supports systematic analysis of how a given policy text pushes a model toward, say, patient confidentiality or toward disclosure to protect third parties.

The headline result is that no constitution wins everywhere. Effects are dimension-selective and model-dependent, so a policy that improves justice reasoning may degrade autonomy reasoning, and the same policy can help one model while hurting another. There is no universal 'ethical' prompt to copy.

To make this usable, the authors propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that picks a constitution per model. It reportedly matches the best per-model choice, guarantees a worst-case floor, and generalises to unseen models at low cost, turning a messy finding into a deployable routing rule.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes alignment policy as a per-model configuration problem rather than a universal document, which complicates the current habit of publishing one constitution as a product-wide promise. It also suggests vendors should ship evaluation harnesses that test policy variants, not just the shipped default. For developers, especially those fine-tuning or self-hosting open models in health contexts, the practical lesson is that copying a well-regarded constitution is not safe: the same text can shift behaviour in unintended directions on a different base model, so per-model validation and a fallback option matter. For clinicians and patients, the finding implies that two tools built on identical ethical language may behave differently at the bedside, and that claims of 'ethically aligned' medical AI deserve scrutiny about which model the policy was tuned for.
report.tools: Watch the MedConstBench paper and its MedDilemma dataset on arXiv and Hugging Face for release details. To experiment, pair open models with existing evaluation harnesses such as EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness or Stanford HELM, and compare published policy documents such as Anthropic's constitution and OpenAI's Model Spec as ready-made constitution variants. Medical question sets like MedQA and MedHELM give a factual baseline against which to measure the ethical shifts.
